clue.text: Manage funds badly? Trouble!

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so the letters before it come out in a messed-up order

blocks.note: both words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: An accountant mishandling the money is asking for trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark signals that the trouble is not financial at all; the whole of 'Manage funds' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is used ironically for a messy, troublesome situation, as in 'there were fun and games at the meeting'.

clue.text: Type of government journalist gets wild about

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: feral means untamed, gone wild
ED is short for editor, the crossword's stock journalist

explanation.surface: A political writer gets heated about the system of government.
explanation.definitionFit: A federal system divides power between a central government and member states, so it names one model of rule.

clue.text: Fool head

blocks.note: first meaning: a silly person
second meaning: informal word for the head or brain

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like 'fool' as a verb with 'head' as its object, but the two words are separate meanings of one slang word.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally the word means both a simpleton and the head or brain, two senses listed in any dictionary.

clue.text: Men up dancing with model and John le Carré?

indicators.note: dancing letters move about the floor and end up in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A party scene: men get up to dance with a model and the spy novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: John le Carré was the pen-name of the writer David Cornwell, so he is an example, hence the question mark. 'With' simply joins the two fodder words.
explanation.definitionFit: A pseudonym an author writes under; le Carré is a famous example of one, so the definition works by example.

clue.text: Racket sport

blocks.note: first meaning: a scheme or line of business, often shady
second meaning: a contest played for fun

explanation.walkthrough: Together the words suggest a racket sport like tennis, but 'Racket' means a scam here.
explanation.definitionFit: The word can mean a dodge or line of work ('what's your game?') and also a match or sport.

clue.text: King tucked into fruit, very last from apple tree

indicators.note: a thing tucked into another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other
the last from a word is its final letter only

blocks.note: a tropical fruit
R is short for Rex, Latin for king
standard abbreviation for very
final letter of apple

explanation.surface: A recipe image of fruit and the very end of an apple, with a king somewhere among them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apple tree' reads as one item, but 'apple' only supplies its last letter and 'tree' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A mangrove is a tropical tree growing in coastal swamps, so it is simply a kind of tree.

clue.text: Son put down as expert

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
to put down an animal is to kill it

explanation.surface: A son belittled for being a know-all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put down' suggests an insult, but here it means put to death.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone skilled has expertise, so the adjective expert fits as a synonym.

clue.text: Spooner's embarrassed bellow in dropping-off place?

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of neighbouring words

blocks.note: embarrassed is red-faced and a bellow is a boom; swap their first sounds

explanation.surface: A blushing shout in a place where people get dropped off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dropping-off' sounds like a taxi rank or drop-off zone; it means dozing off.
explanation.definitionFit: Dropping off means falling asleep, and the room you sleep in is where you do it, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Suffer defeat – I'd bust teeth fighting

indicators.note: in a fight things get knocked about and out of their places, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: all three words as fodder, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A boxer admitting he'd break some teeth in a fight and lose.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to fall, be killed or be beaten, so losing a contest matches it.

clue.text: Family welcomed by chap with one item of clothing

indicators.note: a guest welcomed by a host follows the host in, so this piece comes after the next one

blocks.note: a chap is a man
kin are one's relatives
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Relatives greeted by a man bearing a single piece of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with one' adds the numeral after the container is built.
explanation.definitionFit: A mankini is a skimpy one-piece men's swimsuit, so it is a garment.

clue.text: Embody procreation, possibly

indicators.note: possibly means this is just one arrangement the letters could take, so they may be reordered

blocks.note: taken as written for fodder

explanation.surface: Making babies as a way of giving something bodily form.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to include something as part of a whole, giving it a body or form.

clue.text: Hard to get into bird book?

indicators.note: getting into something means going inside it

blocks.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
trillers are a group of Asian and Pacific birds, or anything that trills

explanation.surface: A novel about birds that is difficult to get into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard to get into' reads as a judgment on a book, but it splits into H plus the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A thriller is an exciting suspense novel, so it is one kind of book, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Cavort in short dress around centre of Ealing

indicators.note: a short word has been cut, losing its final letter
the centre of a six-letter word is its middle pair of letters
one piece is placed around the other, enclosing it

blocks.note: a frock is a dress
the middle two letters of Ealing, a London district

explanation.surface: Someone prancing about in a short dress in Ealing, a London suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: FROCK loses its last letter before going round the middle pair of Ealing.
explanation.definitionFit: To frolic is to play about merrily, so it is a straight synonym of cavort.

clue.text: Seafood platter?

blocks.note: surface reading: a dish of fish and shellfish served at a meal
setter's reading: 'the main' is an old word for the sea, so a dish of food from the sea is a course from the main

explanation.walkthrough: The main is a poetic word for the open sea, so a platter of seafood can be read as the central dish of a dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal dish of a meal is its central course, and a large fish platter could well serve as one.

clue.text: Type of force mentioned in lecture

indicators.note: something mentioned is spoken, so the sound of the word counts, not its spelling

blocks.note: torque is a turning force; in a non-rhotic British accent it sounds like the answer

explanation.surface: A physics lecturer mentions a kind of force.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English without a sounded R, torque and the answer are pronounced alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A talk is a spoken address to an audience, the same as a lecture.

clue.text: Save dollar touring country

indicators.note: touring means travelling around, so the letters wander from their places

blocks.note: both words as fodder

explanation.surface: Advice for a budget traveller to keep cash while touring a nation.
explanation.walkthrough: Neatly, El Salvador uses the US dollar as its currency.
explanation.definitionFit: El Salvador is a Central American nation, so it is an example of a country.

clue.text: Rubbish parroted in Arnie film

indicators.note: rubbish as a verb means to trash or wreck, so the letters are messed up

blocks.note: taken as written for fodder

explanation.surface: Nonsense lines repeated word for word in a Schwarzenegger movie.
explanation.walkthrough: Arnie is Arnold Schwarzenegger, star of the 1987 jungle action film.
explanation.definitionFit: Predator is a 1987 action film starring Arnold Schwarzenegger, so it names one of his films.

clue.text: Cliff's bad temper can lead to squabbles

indicators.note: the lead of a word is its opening letter
bad letters are spoilt and so come out in a wrong order

blocks.note: taken as written for fodder
opening letter of squabbles

explanation.surface: A man called Cliff has a bad temper that leads to rows.
explanation.walkthrough: Cliff looks like a person's name; it is the definition, and 's is 'is'. 'bad' sits beside 'temper' as if describing it, but it governs the letters of 'temper can' plus the S.
explanation.definitionFit: An escarpment is a long steep slope or cliff face, so it is a synonym for cliff.

clue.text: Gossip, drinking port in carriage

indicators.note: something drinking takes a thing inside itself

blocks.note: chat is idle talk
Rio de Janeiro, the Brazilian port

explanation.surface: Someone chattering and sipping port wine while riding in a coach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' tempts as the wine, but it is a seaport city here.
explanation.definitionFit: A chariot is a horse-drawn vehicle, in ancient warfare or later as a light four-wheeled carriage.

clue.text: Capital of Czechoslovakia?

indicators.note: the capital is literally part of the next word, contained within its letters

blocks.note: letters five to eight of Czechoslovakia

explanation.walkthrough: The capital of Czechoslovakia was Prague, but the question mark says read 'of' literally: a capital found in the word itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Oslo is the capital city of Norway, so it is an example of a capital.

clue.text: Tommy maybe flogged fine art occasionally

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: flogged is slang for sold
the second, fourth and sixth letters of fine art

explanation.surface: A British infantryman who sold off some fine art now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy, from Tommy Atkins, is the old nickname for a British private soldier. Flogged here means sold, not whipped.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tommy is a British private soldier, so the definition is an example, signalled by 'maybe'.

clue.text: Puts up with soldiers in a daze

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
OR stands for Other Ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Someone tolerating the troops while half-conscious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puts up with' looks like a single verb meaning tolerates; it splits into the reversal and a plain 'with'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupor is a state of near-unconsciousness, the same as a daze.

clue.text: Reportedly, you look for African nation

indicators.note: reportedly means as said aloud, so the sound of the phrase matters

blocks.note: a gander is slang for a look, as in 'have a gander'

explanation.surface: A rumour that you are searching for a country in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: To have a gander is British slang for to have a look.
explanation.definitionFit: Uganda is a landlocked country in East Africa, so it is an example of an African nation.

clue.text: Cultivate area on hill, producing food

indicators.note: placed on something here means set into it, enclosed by it

blocks.note: to till is to work the soil
A is the abbreviation for area
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Farming land on a hillside to grow something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky hilltop, a word common on Dartmoor in south-west England; 'on' here means placed after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tortilla is a flat bread or, in Spain, an omelette, so it is a kind of food.

clue.text: Leading walk, miles away

indicators.note: away means removed, so the abbreviation for miles is taken out

blocks.note: to march is to walk in step
M is the abbreviation for miles

explanation.surface: Someone at the head of a march while others fall far behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading' looks like part of the walk, but it is the definition, an adjective as in arch-rival.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective or prefix arch means chief or principal, as in archenemy, matching leading.

clue.text: Game that might be a bit of a blow?

blocks.note: first meaning: the party game of tangled limbs on a coloured mat
second meaning: a tornado, a violent windstorm

explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit of a blow' sounds like a setback, but it means a gust of wind, understated with a question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Twister is a party game, and twister is also American slang for a tornado, a very strong wind.

clue.text: Agent with hat is cold-blooded type

blocks.note: a rep is a sales representative or agent
tile is old slang for a hat

explanation.surface: A hatted salesman is a heartless sort.
explanation.walkthrough: Tile is dated British slang for a hat, especially a top hat or bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: Reptiles are cold-blooded animals, and the word is also used for a cold, untrustworthy person.

clue.text: Beach terror unsettled prominent figure

indicators.note: unsettled means disturbed, so the letters are shaken out of order

blocks.note: both words as fodder

explanation.surface: A shark scare on the beach that rattled a celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively a torchbearer is a leader who carries a cause forward, so a prominent figure in a movement.
